title: Two ways of remembering
hookLine: in the Pali texts Kassapa is the strict forest elder; in Zen he is the one who smiled when the Buddha held up a flower (SN 16; Gateless Gate, case 6)

lines: A CROWD WAITING FOR A TALK.
cards: A crowd on a mountain, waiting for a talk. The teacher comes, sits, and says nothing at all. He just holds up a flower.
The whole gathering stays silent, and then one monk smiles.
That's the scene a Zen collection called the Gateless Gate sets down, and the monk who smiles is Mahakassapa: the same man we've spent this week with, the one in rag robes, eating alone by a wall.
Two pictures of one person, side by side.

teach.b: First, the elder of the Pali texts. In the chapter of discourses gathered around him, Kassapa is the forest monk who wants little and keeps the strict practices into old age.
He can be blunt: asked by the Buddha to teach the monks, he says they've grown hard to speak to, and reports two of them competing over who can talk the most.
And when the Buddha dies, it's Kassapa who calls the elders together so the teaching survives.

Second, the smiler of Zen. In the Gateless Gate, after Kassapa smiles, the Buddha speaks. In paraphrase: I have the treasury of the true dharma eye, a teaching that doesn't rest on words, and I entrust it to Mahakassapa.
Zen remembers this as the teaching passing to Kassapa, not as a speech but as a glance, mind to mind. Third, how the two fit. The flower story belongs to Zen; it isn't told in the Pali discourses.
Theravada Buddhists remember Kassapa through the suttas and their commentaries; Zen Buddhists through this silent moment, and many other stories too. Neither memory needs the other to be wrong.

And both are about a man who doesn't need much: a forest, a worn robe, a bowl of rice, or a flower and no words at all. Fourth, why it matters. Love for someone can hold more than one picture of them.
A grandmother strict with her children and soft with her grandchildren. A friend loud at parties and quiet at a hospital bed. Both are true.

how: Theravada Buddhists honor Mahakassapa as the forest elder of the suttas; Zen and Chan lineages name Mahakassapa as the first ancestor after the Buddha, and teachers retell the flower story.

o: the Buddha's cousin and lifelong attendant
great Kassapa, the elder both traditions honor
the monk who first brought Zen to China

games.q: two pictures of Kassapa: tap the pairs.

s: the flower story is told in the Pali discourses
it belongs to Zen; Theravada remembers Kassapa through the suttas and commentaries.
in the Zen story, the Buddha holds up a flower and says nothing
only after Kassapa smiles does he speak, entrusting the teaching to him.
one picture of Kassapa has to be the wrong one
the two traditions remember him differently, and neither memory needs the other to be wrong.

games.q: you're in the crowd on the mountain. the teacher sits down, holds up a flower, and says nothing. what do you do?
o: wait politely for the talk to start.
ask a neighbor what it means.
games.why: in the Gateless Gate, Kassapa smiles, and the Buddha says he entrusts his wordless teaching to him.

practice: Bring to mind someone you know well, living or gone, and find one picture of them that's stern or serious, then another that's tender, funny or surprising.
Set the two side by side without letting one cancel the other, and without deciding which is the real person. Just let both be true, and breathe with them for a while.

wordCard.voice: Mahakassapa. The name both traditions remember him by: the strict forest elder of the Pali texts and the one who smiled at the flower in Zen. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Mahakassapa, great Kassapa: the name both traditions remember him by (Sanskrit Mahakashyapa).

carryVoice: Your line: both are him. One man, two memories, and neither has to lose. Day seven hundred forty-three, done.
